author: Ingrid of the Riverbank
pages:
#Why Nine?

Visitors from the south often ask why the north is divided into nine holds and not eight, or ten. The honest answer is that nobody planned it. The holds grew the way a frozen lake cracks: along lines of weakness that no one chose.

What follows is my attempt to explain each crack.

#The River Holds

The oldest holds lie along the great rivers, where the first chieftains settled because fish do not care who is king. Their borders follow the water exactly, and to this day a farmer on the west bank pays taxes to a different jarl than his cousin on the east bank.

These holds are prosperous, crowded and full of opinions. Their jarls tend to be merchants first and warriors second, which the mountain folk find suspicious.

#The Mountain Holds

Three holds sit among the high peaks. Their borders were drawn by avalanche and rockslide as much as by treaty. A mountain jarl rules fewer people than a river jarl, but every one of those people can survive a winter that would kill a southern soldier in a week.

The mountain holds are famous for their silver mines, their stubbornness and their refusal to pay any tax that has not been explained to them in person, at length, by the jarl himself.

#The Marsh and the Tundra

One hold is mostly bog. It was granted to a disgraced general as a punishment, and his descendants have spent four centuries trying to turn that punishment into a fortune. They have partly succeeded: marsh herbs fetch a good price, and few armies care to march through mud up to their knees.

Another hold is mostly open tundra, wind and wandering giants. Its jarl lives in the only city for many miles and spends most of her time keeping the farmers and the giants from killing each other over cattle.

#The Hold by the Sea

The last hold faces the northern ocean. Its people still build boats the old way and still speak of the Old Shore as if their grandparents had left it. The sea hold sends more sailors and fewer soldiers than any other, and its jarls have a habit of ignoring the rest of the north until someone tries to tax their fish.

#A Word to the Traveller

Each hold has its own laws, its own guards and its own bounties. A crime in one hold may be forgotten across the border in the next. I do not recommend testing this, but I would be a poor guide if I did not mention it.
